title: Conquest: Weaver Courts Wyrd Knights and Fianna Cavalry Model Review
content:
I've been really enjoying lately the amount of dual kits from Parabellum that allow you to make on of two, quite vastly different, regiments. Earlier I reviewed the Gallowglass, letting you make either a Medium ranged unit, or a Heavy melee variant. Now we come to the funkiest, most little shop of horrors-esque cavalry you ever did see. From, I can only assume, the mind of HP Lovecraft come the noble knights and sneaky ambush hunters of the Weaver Courts.

Wyrd Knight by Trout

The Kit, the Vibes, and the Building

Now, I have and will continue to sing the praises of the unique play styles of these two regiments; the same cannot be said of the design. I LOVE the look of these units so much, the sculpt is simple yet detailed, sleek yet active, and the unique mounts make a formidable sight on the battlefield... But for the love of bugs, I cannot tell which is which. If one committed a crime I would pay you well if you could pick them out in a line up! The mounts are (even more so than my BFFs the moths) identical. You have no options in pose either really so multiple units of these will start to look very same same (I'm looking at you Chios people, be more interesting.) Now, as long as you paint things uniquely and tell your opponent in good time, I see no reason this should be an actual issue in a game; I mean I run all my bugs with no rider on top and I've not had any issues, so can't see this being any more than me being a lil petty that the pretty lion plants aren't unique enough. (Isn't my lobster too buttery?)

As said, the build is super simple, so good work again, Para Bellum. The riders can be a little flimsy so a little care should be taken there, but they don't break nearly as much as the damn moose antlers so that's a win in my books.

Golden Daemon?

For my unit as seen here, I went in on the lion vibes with a bright orange skin, pale mane and some black stripes covering the body. The, almost, sinew like skin made contrast painting very effective here so they were up and ready with a good Zenithal base (Black with grey then white "highlights" dry brushed on,) contrast, and some little layered highlights to finish up. I used mainly the Games Workshop contrast range for this as I enjoy the vibrancy of the griffon hound orange. I added a splash of purple into the mouth for some differentiation in colour and added some fun bushes form Green Stuff World to the base to add to the pouncing and sneaky poses of the models which I think (even with the lack of rider) gives these kittens a really great battle presence!

Wyrd Knight by Trout

Git Good Gaming

Now, both these units give you a similar base stat line with a solid March 8, Attacks 5, Wounds 4, and Evasion 2 to keep them safe from some light to medium sneezes. However both these units are very set apart by their unique special rules. Like most of the roster these days, they both sit in the same season as your warlord giving that flex in play. This works nicely for both as being predominantly melee fighters and harass pieces, all four seasons offer up some nice advantages.

The Knights! The most proud and gallant of elf bugs, these solid Resolve 4 Cav units hit damn hard for their points and with a solid range to boot. For the cheap(ish) price of darts favourite score you get a fast moving, Fluid Formation, unit with a good number of attacks and some flexibility of extra rules. If you can get them a seed pre combat (not hard but very needed) you can drastically up their hitting power. At a glance five attacks with no cleave at Clash 3 is fine, but not ground breaking. However, with one seed, you can go from 16 attacks with nothing, to 18 attacks with either Flurry, Cleave 1, or Deadly Blades. This upped hitting power is just insane really. I may sound like a broken record, but the flexibility given by this rule allows you to optimise for the opponent you're engaging. Need a lil AP? Great, you got it! Or just roll terribly and need a mulligan? Amazing! I've seen these cats one shot so much with a Charge-Clash to up-trade very efficiently if used well. The fluid formation allows you that extra threat range, letting you pop into line of sight, or sneak a flank charge in; and the 3 impact hits each at Clash 3 do really add up! Now, you cant expect them to take much of a hit. Wounds 4 and only E2 with no other defensive rules make them disappear to most counter punches. Resolve 4 is nice, but really the damage is done already... But, they're fast and flexible, you should be getting the first strike off allowing you to make the favourable engagements most of the time. A top tier unit I would expect to see 1 (or 5 - really, look at this year's Chios lists) in every Weaver army

Wyrd Knight by Trout

The younger sibling comes in at a budget 160 and a similar stat line. Notably though only Clash 2. Now, the story and lore of the ambush predators, stalking their prey. Striking from the shadows and disappearing into the wild... is amazing and I love it. To represent this, the Fianna Cav have a fun set of special rules called Prowl and Pounce. I think, this is the first rule in Conquest that gives stealth to a unit. The opponent cannot draw line of sight to them should they be outside of 8". So no shots, no magic, and no long bomb charges. This is a really big survival boon for the Fianna's over their knightly counterpart. They do loose this rule until the end of the round should any enemy get within 8" so they can be vulnerable to a March-Charge, or the enemy sending in a fast moving scout unit. But this is fun, balanced, and thematic so I really love this rule!

A fun note to add, the unit is still size 2 and can block line of sight to things behind it. So in theory you can hide your main army behind these lions and have everything immune to line of sight based attacks until you get within 8"! Whilst prowling you do loose scoring potential and 2" of your March so, even with your Vanguard 4, you wont be guaranteed those midboard objectives. You can, during your activation, choose to loose the Prowl rule (so you can be seen) but gain Linebreaker and Terrifying 1 until the rounds end. Stack this with Opportunist, you can get some really spooky flank charges with them. However, the Clash 2 really hurts them and, with no fluid, having to be over 8" away, its not easy to get the perfect flank charge off. Even if you do, your Impact hits are much less effective at C2 and no extra rules like Cleave or Flurry mean they really don't punch up like you'd want them to for the amount of effort you no doubt put into the attack. These are a unit that really do enjoy a Summer based army. The shock helping them dish out a bit more serious damage is a really good percentage increase in output so I think I'd recommend that. But for only 20 points more, I think the Wyrd will see a lot more play in the competitive scene.

Final Thoughts

As for the Season, again it will depend on your play style and the rest of your army. Shock and Summer work well for both, that crunching charge is always a good thing to pounce (heheh) onto your opponent. I'm a sucker for Spring personally, I like the speed; 10" with Fluid on the Wyrd gives them really scary attack range, and Clash 3 innate already gives them the high average hits (with potential rerolls) that I do love. Autumn is Autumn; I do like the Mhor Sidhe Cleave Bloom to go alongside then Flurry on the Wyrd to hit very hard, and the culling rule is, as usual, fine in addition. Dread and Winter is probably the weakest here. With the units being low Wounds and usually MSU (Don't wanna give up fluid/ it's hard to sneak a large unit around) that means most attacks into you will remove the unit anyway, the lack of Inspired isn't usually enough to save them.

I've seen talk about adding heroes into the units but I personally like them to run alone, they're cheap enough to slot into most armies and quick and killy enough to win most 1v1s on the flank, and with good speed to quickly relocate should you need them. All in all one very interesting and decent unit, and one top tier sees this most become a staple of most tree-lover's army collections!

title: MTG Star Trek reveals unstoppable Borg Cube card and exponentially spreading Tribbles
content:
Wizards of the Coast has just unleashed a tidal wave of spoilers for the upcoming MTG Star Trek set. Among them were a bunch of spaceships and a Jean Luc Picard that can fetch and charge them up, a lot of doubling effects, and some intriguing sagas named after specific episodes. There's a lot to talk about here, but we're just going to look at four cards here with truly interesting effects.

First up we have The Borg Cube, an expensive spaceship which luckily has affinity for artifacts, which will make it much more castable in a Borg deck. On the turn that you play it, this is just an overcosted removal spell, but if you're able to get it up to 12 charge counters it becomes very scary indeed.

For starters, it's a flying 6/6 that gives all your other artifact creatures flying, letting you swoop in the skies with impunity. On top of that it lets you assimilate the creature you exiled, bringing it back onto the board on your side as a Borg artifact. Plus, if The Borg Cube isn't dealt with it will kill again - each turn where you don't assimilate when you attack, you get to exile your next victim. Overall, a fantastic card, I'm only sad it can't go in the command zone.

Secondly, we have Q, Stacking the Deck. In terms of reading experience, this one's as confusing as any meeting with Q, but here's more or less what it does. You exile a card from your library, and from that point on, any card in your hand can be used as though it's a copy of that card. I bet there's some tricksy ways to abuse this!

Thirdly, it's Troubling Tribbles, a multiplying alien menace which creates more copies of itself each turn - as do those copies. Now it's not just the green players you have to worry about making an unending, exponentially growing horde. The only comfort is that the Tribbles are 0/1s, so their controller will need to put a little work in to find a way to make use of them.

Finally, we have The Kobayashi Maru Scenario, the famous 'no-win' training simulation. Basically, this is blue Demonic Pact. You get to pick a powerful effect each turn, but if it's still on the board in four turns, you'll lose the game. Rather than boons bargained for with demons, the flavor words give the impression of an officer trying all available options, then giving up and having to abandon ship.

Check out the Debut video for yourself to see all the spoilers just shown off - though I'd say you've viewed the cream of the crop already.

title: Magic: The Gathering Puzzlebox – Deathtouch & Planeswalkers with Teyo, Diamondblade Mage
content:
At time of writing, the least popular new Commander from Reality Fracture is sitting at a cool 2 decks. This is no surprise, as in every set released since around the time of Final Fantasy, there's Uncommon or even Common Legends which have abilities that rival core set chaff in their level of insipidity. No one would bat an eye to learn that Zog, Triceraton Castaway is the least-popular Commander from TMNT; things like this just come with the new normal of how Magic sets are designed. As of Reality Fracture, there have been more new Legendary Creatures printed in 2026 than non-Legendary ones, so a few stinkers are expected—why then, today, am I covering Teyo, Diamondblade Mage? It's not an especially glamorous title, but I'd mark him as the most interesting Commander to be the least-popular from a core set, following its release, at least in recent memory. Black Teyo does something remarkably unique, in providing any permanent with Deathtouch for a turn, so while it's understandable to balk at a mana value of 4, there's some really neat things to be done with this jaded geomancer! Let's get into the pitch.

This is part of a shortform Magic series where I’m covering rapid-fire concepts about Commander that I couldn’t cover in a full Commander Focus, so if you like what you see, certainly let us know!

Deathtouch-a-Touch-a-Touch-a-Touch Me

Teyo's a Flash 3/1 for 4 that upon entry provides a permanent you control with Deathtouch until the end of the turn, with two riders depending on the type that permanent is. If it's a Creature, it gets a +1/+1 counter, but more interesting is that Planeswalkers receive a Loyalty counter. The most common way you're adding Loyalty to Planeswalkers in Black is via Proliferate, so it's very cool to see another way of doing so in the Command Zone that isn't just Yawgmoth, Thran Physician (good as he is, and certainly a part of the 99). Instead of being a midrangey Creature strategy like Doc Yawg, Teyo's all about churning through tokens and wiping the board as often as possible. He's able to convert mass pings from any permanent source into kill spells, and while he of course dies in the process, playing a critical mass of Undying Evil-likes keeps him coming back again and again. Pestilence is probably the example you're thinking of, but that goes away if it sees an empty board, and we can't abide that—I much prefer Noxious Field, which inexplicably turns your Land into a pinger. You probably play both, but it's cool to see how many options exist! Withering Wisps is another banger, as it's quite literally just a Pestilence for 1 fewer mana, so long as you don't need to spend on it in a single turn beyond the number of your Snow-Covered Swamps. While this is of course a focus on Teyo, treat this piece as me begging more Black decks to play the Withering Wisps in its stead, especially if you intent to activate it over a turn cycle, and especially if you're a Monoblack deck. One last aside on this note, we can do something similar via Deathtouch countes and Nesting Grounds, which allows us to pass counters around to any permanent. Black already desires to play nonbasic Land tutors for Coffers+Urborg, so this as a third option to make our things that shouldn't have Deathtouch have it permanently is superb.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

So, Teyo turns these repeatable pingers into boardwipes, big whoop. You do of course hit face when these are activated, most of the time, but with Teyo being 4 mana he's not available at every stage in the game, doubly so if you lack mana for a way to recur him at Instant-speed. This leads us into our next category of card, being payoffs for pinging nonlethally. You may have heard You Are Already Dead called out as the cardname for a Demonic Consultation (my preferred current name is Leave), but here it's actually just a killspell that cantrips. It, alongside its sister card Mirrodin Avenged, are mechanisms by which you can turn the single ping from your Enchantments into proper kills without need of Teyo. There's more than that though, because the pool of 'dealt damage this turn'-matters cards is surprisingly deep, and underexplored in EDH. How about a one-sided boardwipe with Swift Demise? Flexible card draw with Faller's Faithful? Maybe you'd like to teach the table what Haunt does and run a rattlesnake effect like Orzhov Euthanist? Including these cards also makes chump blocking far more effective for both you and your opponents, as any measure of damage can prove fatal while you have mana open.

Liliana et al.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

You know what doesn't die to your Enchantment pingers, though? Planeswalkers. This permanent type is also conveniently mentioned on Teyo himself, as if to remind us, and it provides a proactive play if he's ever dying and re-entering without something worthwhile to give Deathtouch to. Alongside Way of the Necromancer—also in Reality Fracture—Teyo can push Planeswalkers to their ultimates ahead of schedule, while also as mentioned giving you access to consistent full-board wipes. He helps you take out threats, then speed up the clock on the things they'd threaten. Black does of course have Proliferate to help with this, but because a lot of it arrives via Creatures, we need to be careful about how deep the suite is given all these wipes. Of our options, Sorin Markov is likely the best candidate, with Liliana, Death's Majesty close behind: Sorin represents an endgame, especially with our capacity to use his -3 in consecutive turns, and Liliana of course just...gets back Teyo, recouping a Loyalty counter. We can even make a Jace token or two and The Elderspell them away to rush for certain abilities, or power up a Lili with Liliana's Scrounger over a turn cycle or two. Monoblack Superfriends hasn't really been an archetype yet, and Teyo solves a lot of the strategy's issues, albeit at an expensive mana cost.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

The first time I heard about giving Deathtouch to a noncreature, it was maybe 2019, and someone was explaining their Sydri, Galvanic Genius deck, which quite enjoyed Caltrops. Sydri's no longer especially popular, especially with the bevy of new Esper options, but her legacy is retained in looking at Black Teyo. He broadens the options, at a similarly-inefficient cost, but the open-endedness has led to such a fun Scryfall deep dive that I'm unironically considering Desert. 'What are the weirdest ways we can deal damage repeatedly' makes for some fun deckbuilding, and I reckon you'd see cards in Teyo lists that appear nowhere else, were he to find a few dedicated pilots. There's essentially no information on this guy online, no hype, no real coverage; with a cool 2 decks on EDHREC at time of writing, the door is open for someone to make the Teyo list. I haven't committed to banging out a 99 just yet, hence his coverage being on The Puzzlebox and not a full Commander Focus, but dear reader if you're interested in that, let me know. I wager your pod or LGS could learn to fear an 'oops all boardwipes' deck that actually has a Planeswalker win condition. This isn't just another Child of Alara pile, it's potentially something groundbreaking. We'll see who has the Last Laugh.

title: Warhammer 40k 11th edition has a Deathwatch problem
content:
The Paris Wargame Expo kicked off on October 17, and so began our first major Warhammer 40k tournament weekend since the Space Marines codex dropped on the 3rd. The biggest development is that this new marine-powered meta seems to have an issue with the Deathwatch, specifically with them showing up in Space Marine armies and being just a little busted.

Some Deathwatch players were understandably a bit grumpy that the 1DP detachment with their name on it was actually a detachment for other Space Marine players that let them use all the Deathwatch's best toys. Now the evidence suggests that the Deathwatch Support detachment, giving other chapters 500 points of DW to play with, is really damn strong.

Throw some Deathwatch Terminators with their extra plasma cannons into, say, an Ultramarine army, and it turns out it does wonders for their win rate. The Deathwatch Support rules let you throw Precision, Sustained Hits or Lethal Hits onto the units, giving them an absurd amount of killiness, even before you load on your other Space Marine buffs and detachments.

While Space Marines as a whole seemed to be in a pretty perfect spot, with a 51% win rate last weekend, Goo- I mean, Tabletop Battles, ran the numbers and concluded that Marines with Deathwatch in tow were winning 69% of their games. Yowza. Deathwatch alone did decently too - but appeared in such low numbers that we can't really draw conclusions from the available data.

It seems likely that if this pattern continues, Games Workshop will step in and make some tweaks. It shouldn't be too hard to figure out a fix. You could add heavy weapon limitations to the detachment, make it more expensive, stop other detachment rules from working with the Deathwatch units - there's all sorts of options. In other words, don't drop everything and buy a bunch of models with the plan to dominate competitive tables with this technique.

Another high-performing Warhammer 40k faction in the past couple of weeks is the World Eaters, using lots of Berzerkers, while the Astra Militarum is doing dismally - win rates below 40%. Auspex Tactics just released a breakdown if you want all the latest data.

title: 11th Edition Detachment Focus: Hexwarp Thrallband (Updated October 20, 2026)
content:
In our Detachment Focus series we talk about the game's Detachments, covering what’s in them, how they play, and how they’ll fit into the broader meta and your games. In this article we're covering the Hexwarp Trallband for the Thousand Sons.

The Thousand Sons' Grotmas Detachment wasn't much to look at when it first released, owing in part to the army just having better options everywhere else. That was a different story upon the release of 11th edition, particularly when the Detachment was only 2 DP. Opinions on it have cooled since, though it still has some play with the current army, thanks to some decent stratagems and enhancements.

Changelog:

  • 2026-10-20: Updated with revised Detachment Points cost
  • 2026-07-14: Updated for 11th edition.
  • 2024-12-04: Initial publication

Detachment Cost: 3 DP

Force Disposition: Take and Hold

The Hexwarp Thrallband is all about your Psychic characters, giving you buffs to Psychic Attacks and powering you up based on your control of objectives in the middle of the table. To that end, the Detachment features a rule similar to the Chaos Daemons’ Shadow of Chaos, giving you re-rolls on 1s to wound normally with psychic attacks and +1 to wound instead if you control more than half of the objective markers in No Man’s Land. You'll also get bonuses to a number of your stratagems if you use them on units which are in your Flow of Magic.

This Detachment was a bit of a dud on its initial landing; it was forced to compete with the far superior (and outright busted) Cult of Magic Index Detachment in tenth edition. And it also just has some real stinker rules which don't make sense given what's on the army's datasheets. It had a second life in 11th edition as a 2 DP Detachment, but has largely fallen behind Grand Coven and Rubricae Phalanx following its nerf to 3 DP. Hexwarp + Ritual of Regeneration was just too good for this world, it seems.

Detachment Rule: Flow of Magic

Specific areas of the battlefield can be within your army’s Flow of Magic. Your deployment zone is always within your flow. At the start of any phase, if you control at least half of the objective markers in No Man’s Land, until the end of the phase, No Man’s Land is in your flow of magic. At the start of any phase, if you control at least half of the markers in your opponent’s zone, then until the end of that phase, your opponent’s zone is in your army’s Flow of Magic.

When you make a Psychic attack with a Thousand Sons model in your army, re-roll wound rolls of 1. If that model is wholly within your army’s Flow of Magic, add 1 to the wound roll instead.

At first glance, you’re likely wondering why you’d even want this rule - after all, your characters attached to Rubrics already have the ability to re-roll 1s to wound. And getting +1 to wound is neat but not as good as getting full re-rolls to wound, particularly when many of your good Psychic attacks have either ANTI-INFANTRY 4+ or ANTI-MONSTER/ANTI-VEHICLE 4+, making +1 to wound kind of pointless against them. There’s some marginal upside here for Magnus, who wants to be able to re-roll 1s to wound, but that’s pretty small and as soon as he’s within your Flow he loses any benefit from this Detachment. And note that the +1 to wound is instead of the re-roll 1s, not in addition to.

When this Detachment first released, we were not kind to this rule, and with good reason: It's utility is pretty marginal outside of Magnus and Daemon Princes and you'll usually want re-roll 1s to wound over +1 to wound unless you're taking on knights. But it does have some use. That said, your main value here is going to come out of the Stratagems - that's really where being in your army's flow of magic matters. We really, really wish they'd fixed this rule when nerfing the Detachment to make up for it suddenly being 3 DP but well, here we are - no one seems to care enough to correct this.

Credit: Robert "TheChirurgeon" Jones

Enhancements

The Enhancements here are okay (except for the Noctilith Mantle), but only okay. You're not likely to end up taking them in most games.

  • Arcane Might (20 points) – Add 1 to the Strength characteristic of Psychic weapons equipped by models in the bearer’s unit, or add 2 while the bearer’s unit is wholly within your Flow of Magic. This only really matters on your Daemon Prince, in part because his melee attacks are PSYCHIC, and this can get him to S10 - a powerful break point. It's not so much worth it on the other units, where most of the psychic attacks you're throwing out rely on ANTI-whatever. It could be cute on an Infernal Master, where you'd be tossing out S8 Fires of the Abyss.
  • Empowered Manifestation (20 points) – While the bearer’s unit is wholly within your army’s Flow of Magic add 6” to the Range of Psychic abilities the bearer has which specify a range (including Rituals), and each time the model takes a Hazardous test for a psychic weapon, you can re-roll the result. In terms of unit abilities, this is an extremely narrow upgrade - by my reckoning it only does anything on a Daemon Prince or a Terminator Sorcerer. On the latter it lets you get your re-rolls to hit at 24” instead of 18”, which is OK. On the former however, it lets you extend the range on the Daemon Prince’s Stealth aura to 12”, which used to be great but is a lot more trivial in 11th edition. Instead the value here is +6" on Rituals, which means 24" Doom Bolt and being able to launch things from the Sorcerer on Disc without being shot back.
  • Empyric Onslaught (25 points) – While the bearer’s unit is wholly within your army’s Flow of Magic, add 3 to the Attacks characteristic of Ranged Psychic attacks equipped by the bearer. This is a solid upgrade on a Psychic character but works particularly well on a Sorcerer, where moving to 9 attacks base on his [SUSTAINED HITS 3] gun is really good even before you fire up his once per game ability to give him +3 Strength and +3 attacks. Pair that with full re-rolls to hit from your ritual and fish for 6s, throwing out 12 attacks with Lethal Hits and Sustained 3. On average your 12 shots will score something like 20 hits. That said, the requirement to be within your army's Flow of Magic is a real problem in some matchups and 25 points is a lot to pay for something which only has conditional value.
  • Noctilith Mantle (15 points) – While the bearer’s unit is on the battlefield, it is wholly within your army’s Flow of Magic. Models in this unit cannot be selected to use any Rituals. That’s a hell of a downside for a unit, and absolutely brutal in most cases, and you’ll need to do some careful tricks to make sure another unit can hit you with a ritual so you can still Temporal Surge or get a free Stratagem. And then you ask yourself if all this is worth +1 to wound on your psychic attacks, and you realize that no, it probably isn't. If you have the points, the best place for this is going to be on a Daemon Prince or Winged Daemon Prince, where you want to range out wide from your army and you have both a ranged and melee psychic attack worth buffing - getting +1 to wound on the Hellforged weapon against vehicle/monster targets is a better deal than re-rolling 1 to wound, even with dev wounds in play. 

These are some interesting Enhancements, but on the whole their uses are just a bit too narrow to make them "keepers."

Credit: Robert "TheChirurgeon" Jones

Stratagems

Here’s where the real power is in this Detachment. There are some very good Stratagems here, with some solid utility and defensive buffs. They’re all set at a cost of 1 CP, meaning you can get them free with Echoes of the Warp Cabbalistic Ritual.

  • Warding Hex (Epic Deed, 1 CP) – Used in your Command phase to sticky an objective in your army’s Flow of Magic that is within range of one of your PSYKER units. The hoop to jump through here is rough - most of the time it’ll mean holding two objectives midtable before you can sticky anything in No Man’s Land, but you can use this to sticky your home objective early and leave it behind on the few missions where that matters. This can be helpful if you're playing Take and Hold and know you're going to get killed off an objective.
  • Wrath of the Doomed (Strategic Ploy, 1 CP) – Used in the Fight phase after an enemy unit picks targets. Choose one unit they picked as a target and until the end of the phase, every time a model in your unit dies, roll a D6 and add 1 if the unit is wholly within your army’s Flow of Magic. On a 4+, they can fight on death. This is cute but the reason you’re not charging into combat with your models is that they’re generally bad at it. This is best used on some Scarabs but most of the time you’re better off avoiding combat or dying since losing multiple Scarabs in melee is going to ruin your day and they tend to be disappointing when they fight.
  • Strands of Time (Strategic Ploy, 1 CP) – Used in your Movement phase, after a unit Falls Back. They can still shoot or Declare a Charge this turn. If they’re wholly within your army’s Flow of Magic, they can do both after falling back. You’ll almost never want to charge back into combat after Falling Back with a Thousand Sons unit, so that second rider isn’t super important, but being able to Fall Back and shoot is a key ingredient missing from the Grand Coven and it’s super useful to have for a unit of flamer-toting Rubrics or Scarabs, neither of which want to be tied up in combat when they could be shooting things to death. You're going to use this one a lot, and it's the most important Stratagem in the Detachment. Scarabs desperately need to be able to disengage from combat and still shoot.
  • Through the Veil (Epic Deed, 1 CP) – Used at the start of the Reinforcements Step of your Movement phase. You can take one unit of Rubric Marines or Scarabs in reserves and Deep Strike them (the Rubrics gain Deep Strike). If you opted to use this on a unit of Scarabs they can be set up anywhere wholly within your army’s Flow of Magic but more than 6” from any enemy units. If you do this they can’t declare a charge this turn. This is big, and can really help you fit a ten-model unit of Scarabs into some tight spaces. That said, it's important to note that Flow Control checks at the start of the phase, so you can't move onto and steal objectives for Flow, then use this to teleport in closer - you won't be in your Flow of Magic until the Shooting phase.
  • Scouring Warpflame (Strategic Ploy, 1 CP) – Used in your Shooting phase on a Psyker unit in your army’s Flow of Magic. Until the end of the phase, ranged weapons in that unit gain [IGNORES COVER] and after they’ve shot, pick an enemy unit they hit and that unit can’t get the Benefit of Cover for the rest of the phase. This is solid with the changes to 11th edition rules, and its primary uses are stripping cover for a unit of Scarabs or a Forgefiend to put in work with their guns. Rubrics already ignore cover with an icon, so that part is just kind of whatever here, but this can be a big help taking down larger threats.
  • Kaleidoscopic Tempest (Battle Tactic, 1 CP) – Used in your opponent’s Shooting phase, after they pick targets. One PSYKER unit they picked gets Stealth until the end of the phase, and if they’re wholly within your Flow of Magic, they get -3" Detection Range. This was amended to reduce the unit's detection range and it's a good change. A unit in cover with Go to Ground being invisible from more than 9" away is a powerful effect, and can really save your ass.

Look, these are some solid stratagems. The ones you're going to make the most use of are Strands of Time, Scouring Warpflame, and Through the Veil. Being able to fall back and shoot with Scarabs is huge, and they're one of the game's more deadly shooting threats when they can stack buffs.

Credit: Robert "TheChirurgeon" Jones

Playing This Detachment

It used to be you'd take this Detachment because it was a 2 DP Take and Hold Detachment and you could pair it with a busted Sekhetar Cohort or Ritual of Regeneration. These days it's worse for Scarabs than Rubricae Phalanx and worse for your psychic powers than Grand Coven, where you ultimately get a better suite of abilities at the cost of having to run Priority Assets on an army which struggles with unit counts.

As a standalone Detachment, this one is tougher to justify. It's Take and Hold, which gives it an advantage over Grand Coven if you're running low model counts, since Grand Coven's options are Priority Assets (which forces it to take Tzaangors) and Disruption (which is just bad). Hexwarp lists don't really look much different from Grand Coven lists in most regards, but they give you the option of dropping hordes of Tzaangors in favor of just taking big shooty units to do damage and hold space on the table. Winged Daemon Princes have extra value in this Detachment as a standalone unit, and you'll want Magnus as well.

Strengths

  • Fall back and Shoot. This is one of the most useful abilities you can get in Thousand Sons, and being able to do this reliably makes your Scarabs just so much better.
  • Magnus Shooting. This Detachment gives Magnus the ability to re-roll 1s to wound when he’s not in your Flow of Magic.

Weaknesses

  • Weak Detachment Rule. The Detachment Rule is already something you more or less get from Rubrics, and the either/or nature of it suuuucks. Plus it's only on your psychic weapons - and you have no ability to give units the [PSYCHIC] tag on their attacks.

A Sample List

We haven't seen a successful Hexwarp list since the release of Codex Space Marines, but I do like this 3-2 list form Aaron Devost from the Hallowtide Redux GT on October 17. The general notion here is that your three big threats are a Scarab Brick with a Terminator Sorcerer, Magnus, and a Defiler. For my money, the big challenge here is the units count - only 9 units and one of them (Tzaangors) are a backfield objective holder. The three big threats are legitimate, but I worry that the Defiler is eating up too much space, particularly if the list is also sinking 185 points into a Winged Daemon Prince. This is an area where I might play around with Forgefiends or Mutalith Vortex Beasts, as they offer similar levels of output for the same cost or less. This list really feels like it needs 2 more units than it has.

Final Thoughts

Hexwarp Thrallband isn't a great Detachment; it has some decent stratagems but the Detachment rule is pretty lackluster and the enhancements aren't what you'd want to see compared to other Detachments. That said, there are some decent rules here and being able to fall back and shoot is a very big deal for Rubrics and Scarabs. This is a Detachment which you can build around, but whose value is eclipsed by better options.

title: Why I hope Travis Willingham never comes back to Critical Role campaign four
content:
It has been four months since the death of Teor Pridesire. As well as being one of Critical Role campaign 4's biggest story beats to date, it also structurally changed the Dungeons and Dragons game. Three tables became two. And, personally, I think the campaign is a lot more watchable for it.

For a while now, Critical Role campaign four has had a problem of breadth. Expecting 13 actors, however talented, to share a spotlight means some characters fall to the wayside. There's fewer chances to build relationships with a split party, and that lessens investment in their development. Basically, the more characters there are to keep up with, the less time I have to learn to love them.

I mentioned this problem in a recent op ed about the campaign's budding romances. Tyranny and Wick's emotional relationship is engrossing, because they spent a lot of time at the same table, building up to a shared story beat. In contrast, Murray and Kattigan's romance, which bloomed while the two spent months at entirely different tables, felt rushed and flat. The storylines actively suffer when players don't have a chance to collaborate.

What's worse, before the Convergence arc, many characters had no relationship at all. Hal and Tyranny were basically strangers until the Soldiers table disbanded. Heck, in last week's episode, Occtis literally pointed out how little reason characters like Bolaire and Kattigan have to care about him.

Kattigan quickly followed this up by instigating a personal moment between him and the Wizard. And there lies the hidden benefit of reducing table count. The Convergence, and the more intimate tables that followed, have been a chance for the party to really get to know each other.

This has indirectly solved a lot of the campaign's other problems. There are no longer any 'background' characters in the party. Quieter team members like Vaelus and Kattigan are thrust to the forefront more often. Both have had more character moments than ever post-Convergence, and it makes me care about them far more.

Plus, there have been zero filler episodes since The Convergence. This has more to do with the careful planning of Brennan Lee Mulligan, but jumping between fewer tables certainly keeps our attention on the action.

For me, Critical Role does its best storytelling when it focuses on character dynamics in great detail. Episode 39 didn't do much to advance the plot, but the relationship development is what made it a delight to watch. Not every episode can be about the power of friendship, but I'd like to see this attention to detail - to characters as individuals - continue.

That's why, when Occtis chose to be a Wizard instead of a Lord, and not to create a new table, I breathed a sigh of relief. It's why I believe 13 players is simply too many cooks. This current arc has 11 players (while Aabria Iyengar takes some leave). It could support 12, with six players at each table, but I don't think it can support 13.

That means somebody must be cut, and I'm afraid it's you, Travis Willingham. Teor Pridesire was the least directly relevant to the overall story. A new character would likely be more involved, but if I have to choose between the current cast and a character that doesn't exist yet, I know which way I'm leaning.

Travis recently admitted he hadn't prepared a back-up character yet, or thought about re-entering the campaign. Personally, I hope his return never comes. It's nothing against him as an actor or a person. I'd just like campaign four to be slightly less ambitious, not more.

Got your own opinions on Critical Role? Share them in the Wargamer Discord. Or, if you want to do your own roleplaying, why not check out our guides to D&D classes and D&D races?

title: Kings of War: Assembling Your Forces (of Nature), Part 2
content:
G’day Tabletop Battles Readers! I am back again with part two of this series, focusing on building a Force of Nature army for Kings of War. Last time, I was checking out the contents of the King of Champions box for the Forces of Nature, the Ydrin Thorncreeper Company (check it out here). This time, there's actually been some progress, the box has been assembled, and there has been some inspiration and testing of basing schemes. Read on to see.

Ydrin

I went through the assembly of Ydrin last time, but my opinion has only improved. I’m very much looking forward to getting fully into painting him, I'll just have to work out the actual scheme first. I've been watching quite a few Youtube videos on painting Beastmen to get some idea, so while figuring out exactly what my scheme will be, I’ve finished assembling the rest of the box, and got the models primed and ready for colours. I've done my standard priming and zenithal preparation; A spray of Chaos Black from Citadel, then following up with increasingly lighter drybrushing of Neutral Grey, Stonewall Grey and Wolf Grey, all from the Vallejo Game Color line. This gives a nice place to start for a "Contrast Plus" method, which is what I'll be going for. The preparation was done on all the models in the box in the same way.

Ydrin Thorncreeper, ready for painting. Credit: Urr

Centaurs

The Centaurs come as four individual bodies, both horse and humanoid, that match together, while the rest of the pieces are interchangeable. You can build them as Centaur Bray Hunters, the ranged version, or as Centaur Bray Striders, the melee version. I've stuck with the box instructions, and built them as Flaxhoof's Finest, the Bray Striders from Ydrin’s company.

The models all go together nicely, without much complication. A big thing to note about the Centaurs is that they all have good contact points with the bases. Only one body doesn’t have two hooves in contact with the ground, and that one has a nice rock attached to the grounded hoof to extend the support of that leg.

The two-handed weapons are a bit of a pain to match both shoulders and the weapon hands all together, but slow drying plastic glue worked well enough, and this is a problem I don’t think anyone has solved.

Weirdly, the hair comes in a separate piece to the head, which caught me off guard. There's not many pieces per model so it's no big deal. It does seem to work to keep mould-lines off the faces. That has been an issue with some kits in the past, so I'm glad to see that has been solved. Speaking of mould-lines, they really are hard to find on these models . None of them stand out dramatically in the bare plastic and that hasn't changed with a prime and a drybrush.

Tribal Warriors

The Tribal Warriors have also been assembled and prepared for painting. The box comes with two sprues of 10 models each, but this is a mirrored sprue, so there are 5 unique torso & leg pairs, while all the heads and arms are interchangeable depending on how you want to build them. There are enough options to make 10 models of each sort, which can be Tribal Warriors with hand weapons and shields, Tribal Warriors with spears and shields or Tribal Hunters with slings. Again, I’ve built the models for the Champions box, and put together the Swift Shots and the Warriors of the Oak and Ash. I did elect to give the Warriors spears over hand weapons. It won’t make a difference in Champions, but I do like having the Phalanx rule and the extra attacks on my infantry in full size Kings of War.

Much like the Centaurs, these kits go together really nicely. As I was building them, I kept noticing extra details on the models. Little earrings, decorative feathers and lots of straps across the models. This does give me a bit of pause as to whether or not I’ll be able to finish all the warriors before Clash Australia, but that's not going to stop me trying! And if I have to pivot heavily into elementals to get points done quickly, so be it. I’ll be taking the Forces of Nature one way or another.

Basing

While I was waiting for priming weather, I started working on ideas for the bases. I was inspired by a recent trip up to the Victorian High Country at the end of winter, and decided that would be the basing theme of my next army. I then promptly forgot to take as many photos of it as I should have, so enjoy one of the few pictures I could find matching the tundra vibes as a reference.

Tundra Basing Inspiration. Credit: Urr

Off of that, I’ve started out with a few test bases. There’s a few different mixes of basing textures and snow effects, and there was a bit of a learning curve in getting the snow to actually look like snow, but it turns out reading the instructions is a good way to learn to do things properly. I’ve also run off some rocks off of the 3D printer, and am just about ready to commit to the final product. More details on that next time.

Tundra Test Bases. Credit: Urr

November Plans

That’s it for this month. Hopefully soon it’ll be painting time, at least some for some test schemes. While I’m working on that, I’ll be nailing down the final recipe for the bases, and putting together some more models. And in the middle of all this, it's the Australian Kings of War Masters in early November. I won the state's auto-qualifier event this year, so I’ll be joining the Victorian crew and heading up to Sydney to take my shot at the title. Tickets are still available for the side event, Rising, and the more, the merrier. Come along for a great time. Tickets are available here.

title: Lore to Table: Building Salamanders with the 11th Edition Codex
content:
The new release of the 11th edition Codex: Space Marines gave us a ton of new Detachments to play with, including a mix of generic and chapter-specific options to choose from. In this article series, we're going to be looking at different chapters and how to represent them on the table, talking about different combinations and lore-accurate forces.

In our first article in this series, we talked about the Imperial Fists and how I missed subfactions; that's still true, but now we've taken it upon ourselves here at Tabletop Battles to rectify that iniquity a bit by coming up with playable lists that draw heavily from lore inspiration to really show off the different flavors of each Marine Chapter. This time around we're going to be looking at the Salamanders.

The Salamanders represent both an easier and tougher challenge than you'd expect. The obvious starting point is "just take a lot of flamers and melta weapons, problem solved." But as with all of the chapters in our series, there's more to the army to that, and more that's worth exploring. As with the Imperial Fists, we're going to dig a little into the lore of the chapter and find out what other aspects of the chapter we can build around and where the rules help us close those gaps. And as we build, we'll look at competitive lists for our templates where possible - just because we're building to lore doesn't mean we can't kick some ass.

What Kinds of Armies Do We Want to Build?

The Salamanders hail from the burning world of Nocturne and are "a band of warrior smiths and battle artificers, as adept at crafting the tools of war as they are in using them."

The easiest starting point is flamers and meltaguns. The Salamanders are "the flamers chapter," and their basic Detachment - Forgefather's Seekers - plays into this, albeit indirectly, by making your close-ranged attacks +1 Strength. But they're also the chapter of master artificers, who make ornate pieces of wargear and hone their craft to insane levels. The Salamanders are a plenty versatile army, and just as likely to rely on Tactical Squads and Intercessors as any other chapter. They're also known for being sturdy and self-reliant.

I think that there are really two main forces we want to build here, and we can stretch to a third if we really want to:

  • Flameblade - This is our flamer army, full of flamers, meltas, and heavy flamers designed to burn the world. Salamanders Marines are naturally resistant to heat, and that makes them more likely to use flamers and heat-based weapons to defeat foes.
  • Master Artisans - With this army we're going to represent the chapter as master artisans, working on bringing high-end wargear such as relic blades.
  • Elimination Force - This is our stretch goal; a more balanced army meant to show off that at the end of the day, the Salamanders are still a Codex-compliant chapter and bolters do a fine job killing things inside 12".

This gives us three concepts to build around; a short-ranged force filled with flamers and meltaguns, a force filled with master artisan weapons (and thunder hammers, most likely), and a more tactical force focused on mid-range firepower. The good news is that Codex: Space Marines was very kind to the army's flamer- and melta-armed units; Infernus Marines, Flamestorm Aggressors, and melta Eradicators are all units which are not only playable (especially in Forgefather's Seekers), they're downright solid.

Infernus Squad. Credit: Rockfish

Flameblade

The most obvious option, the Salamanders are known for rocking flamers and melta weapons. The good news is that Infernus Marines are very good in 11th edition, and are still interesting (if a bit less potentially jaw-dropping) with the transition to the new Codex. Pyreblasters gaining [BLAST 1] gives them some very nasty output, and they combo well with Eradicators thanks to the ability to strip cover from targets. Getting +1S here on ranged attacks within 12" is a big deal, and we want to combine the unit with the Immolator Enhancement to maximize our output.

Although a bit worse than their pre-Codex incarnation, Flamestorm Aggressors can also be a solid play here, having [BLAST 2] to make up for the loss of D6+1 shots and now with CLOSE-QUARTERS to dig out of problem spots in addition to having power fists, plus they can push to S6 as well by getting within 9" of their target. Eradicators are also just a solid option, and taking short- and mid-ranged units in Impulsors is a solid competitive play.

Jeroen Janssens ran this list to a 3-2 finish at That 6++ GT last weekend, but started 3-0 in the process. It's a list proudly running two Redeemers, each filled with Flamestorm Aggressors, two units of melta Eradicators in Impulsors, Heavy Intercessors, Inceptors, and Scouts. It's heavy on Gravis marines, in part because it's running the Gravis Siege Force instead of Assault Brethren, giving it extra durability against incoming attacks.

Final Thoughts

If you're running Salamanders right now, chances are you're going to run Forgefather's Seekers. It's both thematically appropriate and well, it's just a really good Detachment which encourages you to take some of the army's best units anyways. The Land Raider Redeemer is one of the game's nastiest units, and it remains every bit as nasty now that the flamestorm cannons are 4 shots with [BLAST 2] instead of D6. You're averaging fewer shots, but now you have [DEVASTATING WOUNDS] against smaller targets to make up for it. Overall the Salamanders give you quite a few options for different ways to build, and whether you want to take Impulsors full of flamers or trundling Flamestorm Aggressors, you have options.

title: For the Gods is a divine board game of Greek myth, but it's one step short of epic
content:
Our Verdict

For the Gods! is smooth sailing, with approachable, airtight area majority rules. Rough seas make the best sailors, though, and the game doesn't forget to offer tense strategic decisions. It's not as complex or memorable as some others of this genre, but it's an excellent gateway with an entertaining bag-building spin. Plus, it's simply divine to behold.

Pros
  • Visually lovely
  • Simple yet brutal strategy
  • Beginner-friendly, but fun for veterans
Cons
  • Less fun at two players
  • Relies a lot on luck
  • Theme feels superficial

For the Gods! is the latest title from a trio of star-studded board game designers. Between them, Trevor Benjamin (Mandala, Resist!, Undaunted), Brett J. Gilbert (Mandala, Divinare), and David Thompson (Undaunted, Resist!) have a small army of awards and nominations. That means, for their next project, expectations are sky-high.

That's fitting for a board game about the Greek Gods, though it doesn't take place on cloudy Mount Olympus. Instead, two to four people play as these deities' human worshippers. Your goals are much more mortal: sail the Aegean archipelago, and build taller temples than your religious rivals.

This is an area majority game whose simple rules are as smooth as Grecian marble, but as rich as a wine-dark sea. The core engine is an efficient bag-building mechanic. Everyone starts the game with 24 stones in their bag (with zero to three pips printed on top), and you'll begin with a starting hand of five, hidden behind a privacy screen.

Each turn, you'll choose whether to visit a new region on the stunningly vibrant board. Each stop on your voyage costs a stone, which you'll return to the bag. Once you've reached your intended port, you can choose to establish, elevate, or dedicate a temple.

Establishing means building a fresh temple in that region, while elevating extends an existing structure. When establishing, simply grab a base, and place any number of tiles with matching pips on top. If the region has a god token lying around, throw it straight in your bag.

These god tokens come into play when you dedicate a temple. You can dedicate as part of an establish or elevate action, and it allows you to place a single god token on top of your temple. This adds a fancy cornice, which looks snazzy, but mainly exists to show the value of the pips beneath. More importantly, though, dedicating your temple triggers that god's power.

Four to six random gods form your pantheon, depending on player count. Dedication lets them shake the earth and seas in different divine ways. Athena swaps the location of two temples on a single island, while Ares steals a god token from a rival temple in the same region. Hestia lets you use two types of stones on a single temple, while Hermes straight-up gives you another turn.

Hephaestus and Zeus both add extra foundation stones to your temples, and Poseidon teleports you across the map. Artemis and Aphrodite both give you a chance to collect additional glory tokens - which you can usually only acquire by building a region's tallest (or, sometimes, second-tallest) temple. It's these Glory tokens that decide the game's winner.

The gods are what turn these calm seas into surging, strategic waves. You're no longer just gunning for the island that nets you the most glory. A detour to pick up a powerful god stone could seriously change the board state, and it's worth squabbling over those pieces before they're gone. The fact each game's gods are randomized makes this tactical tempest tough to control, but it also makes this a game worth returning to for repeat plays.

Those aren't the only tricky choices you'll face. Your voyage starts gently, with enough space for everyone to build their towers. Quickly, though, the archipelago grows crowded.

You'll need to decide which Glory tokens to fight over, and what stones you're prepared to spend on that battle. A tower using all of your three-pip tokens is almost guaranteed to win, but that means fewer chances to claim land elsewhere. Plus, do you spend a god token early or late - or avoid spending them at all?

Some, like Apollo and Hermes, trigger additional draws from your bag. And, once someone cannot draw the required number of stones from their bag, end-game triggers. All other players take a final turn, and Glory points are totaled. Triggering end-game isn't a death sentence for your zealots, but it's a disadvantage that could bring your plans crashing down.

For the Gods! is an easygoing, beginner-friendly teach, but the competition is rather brutal. The gods do not suffer misplays. Take your eye off an undisputed region, dedicate at the wrong time, or mismanage your remaining bag, and it's easy to fall behind in the race for glory.

That breeds an environment of tense turns, where your decisions have real impact. The game's reliance on luck occasionally stifles this, as a bad pull from your bag can seriously slow you down. Still, it's a relatively minor frustration. The joy of this game is making the best of the limited turns, space, and stones in front of you.

It's a successful design, but for me, it's not particularly memorable. Area majority is a crowded genre, and many rivals offer more innovation, complexity, and strategic thrill. Plus, there's no clever marriage of theme and mechanics that elevates this above the many, many other Greek mythology board games. For the Gods! is gorgeous, but its theme feels superficial overall.

Those aren't deal-breakers, and I expect many people will love For the Gods! Its simplicity, style, and strategy are impressive, if not ground-breaking. Any minor deity would be happy with this offering.

Want to learn more about the year's best board games? Check out our guide, which I update weekly. Or, poke me in the Wargamer Discord and ask for some more recommendations.

A review copy was provided by the publisher.

title: [StarCraft TMG] Wave 2 Models: Ravagers, Siege Tanks, Immortals, Oh My
content:
It’s a pretty good time to be playing the StarCraft TMG. Between a new balance patch, the updated release schedule, and the previews that have gone up for the November releases, we’ve got quite a bit of meat on our plate. Today we’re going to dig into some of that meat and talk about the new units that came out this month.

Ravagers

Added with StarCraft 2: Legacy of the Void expansion, Ravagers quickly became a fan favorite. A quick-moving psuedo-artillery unit that rewarded micromanagement and allowed Zerg to push entrenched positions earlier, Ravagers function in much the same way on the tabletop. Taken individually or in units of two, Ravagers are Speed 4/8, with an armor and evade stat of 5+, and a comfortable 9 hit points. With the Squadron rule improving their coherency to 4”, in the movement phase Ravagers can perform the Deep Tunnel action, which allows them to relocate at the end of the round to a new position.

Their flagship ability, Corrosive Bile, lets you set up one Corrosive Bile token for each model in the unit within 14” of that model. At the end of the Assault Phase, each unit within an inch of that token will immediately take Hits (5). Their assault phase ranged weapon, Plasma Discharge, is a 4 RoA weapon hitting on 3’s and surging against Light. While respectable, the single point of damage it deals means generally it might be better to get away from the enemy as it probably won’t be doing much.

Credit: Blizzard Entertainment/Archon Studios

Besides the Burrow Ambush upgrade most Zerg units have, their other two upgrades both improve the Corrosive Bile token. Bloated Bile Ducts improves the token's effect range to 3", allowing you to hit more enemy units with it or screen a zone out more effectively. Potent Bile will apply Debuff (Armor) 1, improving how much damage goes through on those hits. Zealots and Marines in particular despise this upgrade. Both of these upgrades are 20/40, making them fairly expensive on a unit of 2, but definitely worth considering and trimming upgrades around as they massively improve the utility and damage of the Ravager.

Placing your Corrosive Bile token near ranged units that have already activated is crucial, as you will subsequently force your opponent to choose between Shooting and taking damage, or Running and wasting their chance to shoot. Deep Tunnel can let you stage to a new position for discharging more bile in the subsequent round. Both of these abilities are performed in the Movement Phase, and you can perform them before or after a move, so setting your Corrosive Bile token then running away with your big Speed stat is a great way to harass enemy units without suffering damage from the enemy in return. Combine this Deep Tunnel, and you’ll set yourself up perfectly to relocate somewhere to reset your Bile Token in the next Movement phase, before moving to safety and beginning the process again. Despite their large hit point pool, Ravagers are very frail on the save and evade stat compared to Roaches, and Marauders and Immortals will love to try to hunt these guys down. Hit and run is the name of the game, and Ravagers are very good at playing it.

Zerg Ravager | Credit: Benjamin "Toll" Scott

Ravagers also come with the Cocoon Tactical Card, with two powerful Movement Phase abilities on it. Ravager Morph is a once per game ability that lets you morph a Roach into a Ravager. Keep in mind this new Ravager will be bereft of any upgrades, so plan accordingly if and when you want to use it. Spawn Larva allows you to perform Respawn (2) on any Size 1 unit, like your Zerglings. Bringing back two models, when combined with the Swarmlings' innate ability to regenerate, can bring 4 or 5 Swarmlings each turn can swing things back your way if the tide begins to turn. While strong, both these abilities come at a cost; Cocoon does not provide a Biomass, so you’ll only be using it for its abilities all game.

Siege Tank

For many players, when asked to think of the most iconic StarCraft unit, it will be the Siege Tank. A combined armored platform and mobile artillery unit, the Siege Tank is great at two things: blowing things up, and blowing lots of things up. Always taken as a single unit, the Siege Tank has a base cost of 220 minerals, but considering the Siege Mode upgrade cost 20 minerals, we can safely consider it a 240 base cost unit. With a Speed of 7, and whopping 14HP, it's reasonably mobile and deceptively tough even considering its mediocre 5+ armour. While not in Siege Mode, the unit passively benefits from the Heavy Plating rule, gaining Tough (1) and vastly improving your saving throws. It also has the Large rule, meaning despite being Size 2 while not in Siege Mode it cannot move through gaps smaller than 3”. This rule also allows the model to pass through, and end its move on, Size 0 or 1 terrain pieces, and if it does either of those things, that Terrain piece is removed from the game. Rolling thunder indeed.

Credit: Blizzard Entertainment/Archon Studios

The Siege Mode upgrade lets you engage Siege Mode before or after your movement, and utilize the Shock Cannon. You can also take the Coordinated Strike upgrade, and target a friendly non-engaged unit on the battlefield. When shooting with the Shock Cannon, you can ignore its range limitation and instead target an enemy unit within 8” and visible to a model in the selected friendly unit, effectively utilizing them as a spotter. These actions are both used in the Movement Phase, so plan accordingly.

In the Assault Phase, while not in Siege Mode, the Siege Tank utilizes its Twin Cannon profile. With a Range of 12”, an RoA of 8, and Pierce 2 and Surge against Armored targets, even without the cannon it can devastate armored targets. It also has a Devastating Charge of (4) 3+, if you need to use that for whatever reason. But the real showstopper is of course the Siege Mode-exclusive Shock Cannon. With a base range of 18” and surging against both Light and Armored targets, the Shock Cannon will delete entire units. Dealing damage equal to the size characteristic of the target, and with RoA of BT+4, you want to maximize how many models you’re hitting, as not only does it increase your RoA but you’ll also surge against every model you hit, denying them armor saves. The only downside to this beast is that it hits on 4+, so you could be prone to a whiff on low dice count.

Credit: Blizzard Entertainment/Archon Studios

In the Movement Phase, stage this somewhere defensible, like near or on a home objective. You don't necessarily need to get it where it needs to go Round 1, but by the end of Round 2’s movement phase it should be in a semi-permanent home. After that, it begins to speak for itself. Use things like the new Factory (Tech Lab) to give it Precision (2) and negate some of those potential low rolls on the 4+. Its Shaped Blast upgrade lets you shoot into engagement range once per game. Very useful if you expect to be going into a combat heavy list, as you can potentially remove your own units from Combat by eliminating the engaged enemy unit, freeing up your own unit to Shoot accordingly. (Condit: Though you will need to be careful since the Spillover rule does mean your own units will take damage if they're caught under the template.) Its final upgrade, Smart Shells, gives you a once per game shot at Long Range 24” and with Indirect Fire. This one can be hit or miss (literally) as the Long Range Shock Cannon will be hitting on 5+. Into something like a swarm of Zerglings, where you’ll have up to 22 Surging rolls, and combined with the Precision from the Factory (Tech Lab) it can soften up targets before they can close the gap.

Immortal

Returning to serve on the tabletop, the last mainline unit in this wave is the Immortal. Dragoon pilots willingly relocated into the Immortal chassis, continuing to share their centuries of combat experience with other Protoss warriors. Like in the game, Immortals serve as Armored hunter-killers, surging against these targets while reducing incoming damage of anything more than 1. With a Speed of 7 they are deceptively quick, and their combined 4+ Save, 6 Shields and 8 Hit Points makes them a difficult target to engage at range.  With their Improved Barrier rule, a 0 PE Reaction, they can reduce incoming damage from a shooting attack to 1, which can be life saving against a Siege Tank which otherwise deals 3 damage per success with no armor saves. Combine this with the ability from your new Robotics Facility card to give you Tough (1) and Dodge (1) and your shields are all but guaranteed to hold.

Credit: Blizzard Entertainment/Archon Studios

With the Indomitable rule, Immortals are blessed with the ability to shoot out of combat, but this ability can be a double edged sword. Enemies can shoot back into it, and whatever it shoots will gain an Evasion roll that the Immortal will not benefit from. The Immortal is vulnerable to being swarmed by Zealots or Zerglings, who can potentially lock it into a very unfavorable combat.

The Immortal really shines when providing fire support against those pesky Armored targets. Its stock weapons, Photon Disruptors, are actually two separate attacking profiles. The Right Phase Disruptor has the Sidearm keyword, allowing you to shoot with both weapons in a phase. Both weapons otherwise share identical stats; a range of 12, a RoA of 4, hitting on 3+, surging D3 against armored targets with a damage of 2, and being able to fire at Long Range 16”. On the downside, they also have the Concentrated Fire (1) meaning they can never eliminate more than a single target during an action, so even firing both will mean you never get more than two model kills on them.

Their upgraded weapon, the Phase Disruptor, can be considered a small upgrade veering on sidegrade. Like the base guns, they have two profiles, one of which has side arms. This weapon trades Long Range 16” and the 2 damage for a base damage of 1 but gains the Pierce (3) Armored rule and loses Concentrated Fire, allowing damage to spill over and eliminate more models. Excellent into swarming armored units like Roaches and Ravagers, who likely will die to single round of shooting, but significantly more anemic into Light targets who will be suffering only a single damage point per success now if these bigger targets aren’t available. You can choose to swap out only a Photon Disruptor for a Phase Disruptor if you wish, and this isn’t a terrible choice into something like Zerg which often will give you multiple targets. Since the weapons batch separately, you can optimize accordingly which units you want to shoot with which weapons. (Condit: The separate batching also means each weapon gets its own Surge die, so even if you wind up firing them both at the same Armoured target you're a little better off than you would have been otherwise.)

Credit: Blizzard Entertainment/Archon Studios

Outside of the weapon upgrades, they also come with two additional ones. Fury Unyielding gives their ranged weapons Critical Hit (1) whenever they are within 3” of an objective, providing another hit that bypasses armor saves, and a must have for anybody who just wants to point their Immortal in a direction and have it remove things. For the Ancients gives you Precision (1) whenever you are shooting a target from more than 8” away. With the Photon Disruptors, this synergizes quite nicely and can help offset Long Range shooting, but may be less useful with the Phase Disruptors as their range is only 12”. But consider things like the Twilight Council tactical card, which can boost your ranged weapons by 4”, and this upgrade may be worth the squeeze even there.

Final Thoughts

Three great new units with three very different niches continue to shape the battlefield in exciting new ways. Ravagers will disrupt your opponents careful positioning, allowing Hydralisks to take shots or Zerglings to charge even as you force them backwards, the Siege Tank provides the heavy fire support your Terran armies crave, and the Immortal will hunt down any armored targets and give them a beat down. The StarCraft Tabletop Miniatures Game is shaping up to be a fantastic addition to our retinue of wargames, and these new units and tactical cards will let you pound your enemies into submission like never before.

title: Bizarre WW1 wargame starring anteaters in trenches gets a brand new starter set
content:
Quar: Clash of Rhyfles, the skirmish wargame inspired by a child's loredump, and featuring WW1-style combat between bizarre anteater-lizard creatures, has had a major facelift, as publisher Wargames Atlantic has just released a brand new starter set.

The redesigned box features the Royalist Creevish fighting the nomadic Western Arnyarans, with models for 12 infantrymen apiece, plus plenty of setting-agnostic terrain. The old beginner box was getting very hard to get hold of, so this new release, which launched Friday, October 16, is going to do wonders for making the title more accessible.

Featuring deep lore incongruous to its strange and cute models, Quar is a casual 'beer and pretzels' style skirmish game with lots of chaos and room for customization. With its narrative focus and particular whimsical-yet-gritty aesthetic, it has something in common with indie darling Turnip28, though of course one major difference is the existence of an official line of models.

The game features a 'pluck' resource system which you can spend to tweak outcomes, and an interesting action system where you don't know at the beginning of each turn how many moves you're going to be able to make. This adds an extra layer of uncertainty to proceedings.

The starter set is retailing for $99.95/£89.95 from Atlantic Games' website. It contains sprues for 12 figures per side (24 in total), the full rulebook, cheat sheets, tokens, dice, market and barricades terrain, and unit cards.

Wargames Atlantic promises more model kits for each of the factions in this box in 2027, along with the freedom-fighting Partisans. Hopefully we can see some vehicles, I want tractors dammit! It's also debuting a whole new mode of play for the game next year, with mass battles - upgrading the skirmish level gameplay into something on a bigger scale.

title: Tabletop Battles Reviews: Warhammer 40K Boltgun 2
content:
Three years ago, Auroch Digital dropped Boltgun, and all was good. Then last week Boltgun 2 was dropped, and all was even better. I purposefully hadn’t followed development for this game outside of what I saw from Warhammer Skulls. I prefer to go into things totally blind for my own sake, but deep down I knew I was going to enjoy this game no matter what.

I’m a sucker for Boomer Shooters, a slave to the genre really, the crazier the better, and Boltgun slots in on the tamer end of the spectrum where games like ULTRAKILL sit on the far other end.

Boltgun 2 is a lot more of the same formulae, and I mean that in a mostly positive way, except that it’s bigger, more refined, and just has a lot more stuff in it. It’s the same fun, you’re sprinting, jumping, charging, shooting, bashing, chopping through really cool arenas while the music team use your weapon noises as background percussion for their screeching guitar riffs.

Where the first game was jumping, chainsword charging and strafing, Boltgun 2 is all about more frantic, twitchy, high-speed carnage where you’re slide cancelling into a slo-mo superjump that lets you empty a Storm Bolter into some bozo in power armour and end his 10,000 year survival streak.

Departing from the first game, Boltgun gives you two characters to play with. I always thought they’d add more characters to Boltgun 1, it seemed set up for it, but it never happened. I don’t know if that was a scrapped plan or not, but they’ve made up for it here. Boltgun 2 pitches two badass heroes of the Imperium for you to play, the returning Sternguard Veteran Malum Caedo, (still voiced by Rahul Kohlui) and the Sister Celestian Nyra Veyrath. (Voiced by Alanah Pearce, who you'd recognise as Malevola from Dispatch!)

Promotional image courtesy of Auroch Digital.

You have different loadout options available to each character, with some crossovers, a different ability each that does the same thing (charging into enemies and making them explode), and a different health/armour pool. The Sister of Battle, Nyra, is generally faster and can jump higher, while Malum can tank more damage overall and has access to way quicker horizontal movement with his charge.

I don’t think there’s so much of a difference between the two that you feel like you’re missing out if you only play once, your mileage will really depend on how cool you find the weapons. But I really don’t think you’re going to play just once though.

The campaign for both characters is the same, but there’s a branching path system so there is a chance to do different levels as either character with the same convergence points through it all. It’s a nice way to make a playthrough of each character feel different, and there’s no weak points along the way either. All the levels kick some serious ass, and it makes hunting down Vashtorr as much fun the second time as it was the first.

The improvements they have made to the gameplay from the first game are small but impactful, like improving the controls to include a weapon wheel instead of relying on hotkeys, and your movement options being expanded to the point that Malum Caedo clearly missed his calling by choosing to be a Sternguard instead of a Vanguard Veteran. (seriously, he can leap across the map with his chainsword. and that's without a jump pack.)

If you’re speedrunning inclined, there is absolutely some heinous tech you can do to start beating levels in stupid quick time. Your level of freedom in leaping around, especially with the enhanced mobility in this game, means you’ll have plenty of fun trying to find skips. This isn’t im-sim levels of shenanigans by any means, it’s still a linear game, but I feel they found various ways players could skip parts of the level in development and just shrugged their shoulders at it.

In addition to Josh's review, Rob and Norman have been playing Boltgun 2 over on the Tabletop Battles YouTube channel:

Not that you want to skip past enemies because the new weapons added to the game are sick. Flamers in Boomer Shooters tend to be underwhelming, but Nyra's version of the flamer acts less like a traditional flamer and more like a pressure-washer of death. It was the most fun weapon to use in the game by far. The Meltagun as well has been revamped from a glorified super shotgun into my new favourite representation of a meltagun to date. It’s a solid beam that deals heavy pulses of damage that totally slag anything in front of you, and it only gets better when you get the multi-melta.

All the art they’ve made for the game is gorgeous, and there’s so much more of it this time around. Boltgun 1 had a limited enemy roster of Tzeentch and Nurgle Daemons, cultists, and Chaos Space Marines & Terminators. Boltgun 2 has the same, and then sprinkles on every Cult Legion for flavour.

You’ll be fighting Berserkers, Scarab Terminators, Noise Marines, Blightlord Terminators, and daemons you didn’t see in the previous game too, like Daemonettes and Bloodcrushers. It’s a lot. You won’t be doing it alone either, as a regiment from the Death Korp of Krieg pops up sometimes to help you out (by soaking up boltrounds, mainly).

Boltgun 2 has a much larger scope to its campaign. Boltgun 1 was set on Graia, a single planet, and there were a lot of fun environments to it but there had to be a unifying motif between levels. Boltgun 2 has you visiting multiple planets, different areas on those planets, voidships both Imperial and Chaos, and it let the level designers run absolutely wild.

There are some ridiculously cool environments in Boltgun 2, and it stands out as one of the things I loved most about the game. You need two playthroughs to appreciate them all, as there’s a branching mission path to accommodate two playthroughs with two different characters, but it’s so worth it. There’s some absolutely badass stand outs, like a Khornate Ziggurat with gore pits, industrial blood pumps, and so many piles of skulls that sit nicely against more traditional Imperium grimdark industrial, like an underwater lab facility or an underhive.

I don’t want to seem like all the new sprite work for enemies and allies didn’t excite me, it did, but the level design was just so fantastic I had to dedicate a big chunk of this review to call it out. Explore those levels. It’s worth it. (And they’re littered with secrets.)

Despite how cool it was to see all the legions in the game, I found the variety worked against the game. Boltgun 2 is a brisk experience; I got it done twice in about 12 hours on Hard mode. There’s a good chance you’ll only encounter a type of enemy for two campaign missions at most, and that sucks.

I think the game could really have benefited from some kind of Codex that stored enemies you encountered so you could read about their mechanics and check out their sprites up close. It’s a small gripe because it feels like a ‘my lobster too buttery, my steak too juicy’ type of complaint but I just liked some enemies more than others, and wanted to keep fighting them more.

This game is well worth a buy if you’re a fan of this genre, and a great first try if you’re Boomer Shooter curious. It’s a short, sweet, and gentle introduction to the craziness of this type of game. Obviously if you’re a Warhammer fan this game will speak to you on a lot of levels; the art, the story, the vibes are all immaculately Warhammer but if you’re just someone who wants a shooter, it’s totally sick. Is it a great intro to the setting? Not particularly, it doesn’t explain much, but it doesn’t need to.

I think it’s a shame it took three years to come out but hopefully they open a pipeline to get more content into the game, some DLCs, or some workshop support would be great. Games like this can live forever with a level editor, just look at what people are still doing with GZDoom.

For the price tag, I’d find it hard to regret picking it up. If you’re into replaying games, there’s a lot to do between trying harder difficulties, 100% secrets on both characters, and speedruning especially I think can be a massive draw for this game in particular. There are some great tools available to do skips and I’m excited to see people find them out.

If you’re someone who is one and done, I think you’ll be satisfied too. Getting to that final boss fight and hearing Mick Gordon make a guitar growl and snarl at you before you unleash all the weapons in your arsenal is more than satisfying one time over.
